meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'In politics, nothing happens by accident. If it happens, you can bet it was planned that way'?
meta.ogDescription: Not FDR. The line turns up in Gary Allen's 1971 conspiracy books, probably a twist on Roosevelt's 1935 Citadel line 'we are planning it that way.'

answer.label: Not Franklin D. Roosevelt — a 1970s misquotation
answer.authorDates: 1936–1986 · American conservative writer, John Birch Society spokesman
answer.sourceLine: There is no record of Roosevelt saying this. The earliest uses Barry Popik records are in two 1971 books by Gary Allen, including None Dare Call It Conspiracy, which credits it to “FDR” with no source. Wikiquote calls it most likely a garbled form of FDR’s 1935 Citadel remark, “we are planning it that way.”

source.heading: Where the line actually turns up

docMeta.dd: Rossmoor, CA: Concord Press, 1971 (Popik quotes the 1972 printing, p. 8)
Remarks at the Citadel, Charleston, S.C., 23 October 1935: “we are planning it that way”

source.excerpt: FDR once said “In politics, nothing happens by accident. If it happens, you can bet it was planned that way.” He was in a good position to know. We believe that many of the major world events that are shaping our destinies occur because somebody or somebodies have planned them that way.
trail: Wikiquote ↗ lists the line under Roosevelt’s Misattributed quotes: there are “no records” of him saying it, and it is “most likely a misquotation” of his 23 October 1935 Citadel remarks.

Roosevelt’s real words are in the American Presidency Project transcript ↗: “Yes, we are on our way back—not just by pure chance… We are coming back more soundly than ever before because we are planning it that way.”

Barry Popik ↗ (15 December 2012) quotes the line from Gary Allen’s Richard Nixon: The Man Behind the Mask (1971, p. 67) and None Dare Call It Conspiracy (1971, p. 8). He then follows it through letters to newspaper editors from 1972 to 1978.
Metabunk ↗ reaches the same conclusion, citing the researcher Loren Collins. It also notes that “We Planned It That Way” became a 1938 anti-FDR slogan.
source.excerptNote: Allen gives no source for the “FDR” line. What Roosevelt actually said at the Citadel in 1935 was about economic recovery: “We are coming back more soundly than ever before because we are planning it that way. Don’t let anybody tell you differently.”

author.name: Gary Allen
author.heading: About Gary Allen
author.metaLine: 1936–1986 · American conservative writer & John Birch Society spokesman
author.bio: Gary Allen was a California writer, a spokesman for the John Birch Society and a contributor to American Opinion. In 1971 he co-wrote None Dare Call It Conspiracy with Larry Abraham. The book argued that an “Insider” elite plans world events, and it is the earliest place Barry Popik found this line with this wording. Allen is the earliest known user of the line and the person who pinned it on FDR. No one has shown that he coined it.

copyAttribution: "In politics, nothing happens by accident. If it happens, you can bet it was planned that way." — Misattributed to Franklin D. Roosevelt; earliest known in Gary Allen, None Dare Call It Conspiracy (1971). FDR's real line (Citadel, 23 October 1935): "we are planning it that way."

misattribution.heading: How a recovery boast became a conspiracy slogan
misattribution.intro: The line is everywhere on quote sites and in “thought for the day” columns, always credited to FDR. The record shows it first being pinned on him in 1971 conspiracy literature, some 26 years after his death.

items.why: Wikiquote ↗ says there are no records of Roosevelt saying it. His closest real line, at the Citadel on 23 October 1935, credited the economic recovery to planning: “we are planning it that way.”

Allen credits FDR with the line in two 1971 books, with no source given: first as “Nothing just happens in politics. If something happens you can be sure it was planned that way,” then in the now-familiar wording in None Dare Call It Conspiracy (Popik ↗).
Readers repeated the “FDR” line in letters to the Daily Inter Lake (1972), Dallas Morning News (1972), Telegraph Herald (1974), Boston Herald American (1976) and Omaha World-Herald (1978) (Popik ↗).
Popik ↗ notes that Kennedy said “There are no accidents in politics” in 1960, just after his son John F. Kennedy won the presidency.
Metabunk ↗ reports that Knox used “We Planned It That Way” as the title of a 1938 pamphlet attacking FDR. That turned Roosevelt’s recovery line into a jibe against him.

misattribution.truthLine: Roosevelt said “we are planning it that way” about the economy in 1935. The conspiratorial “nothing happens by accident” version is not his. Its earliest known appearance is Gary Allen’s 1971 books (Popik ↗; Wikiquote ↗).

context.heading: Why the twist matters
lead: Roosevelt’s Citadel remark was a campaign-season boast that the New Deal’s planning, “not just by pure chance,” was bringing the country back (transcript ↗). The popular quote reverses that point. Credited to a president who was “in a good position to know,” as Allen put it, it becomes inside testimony that hidden planners run events.
That is why the line keeps circulating. It lends a famous name to a conspiracy-theory view of history. Neither Wikiquote nor Popik found any Roosevelt source for it.
context.pull: “We are coming back more soundly than ever before because we are planning it that way.” — FDR, 1935
